facts.statement: Canadian paleontologist Michael J. Ryan first coined the name Medusaceratops in a dissertation in 2003.
facts.quote: The name Medusaceratops was coined by Canadian paleontologist Michael J. Ryan of the Cleveland Museum of Natural History in 2003 in a dissertation.

facts.statement: The genus was formally described by Ryan, Russell, and Hartman in 2010, with the type species Medusaceratops lokii.
facts.quote: Medusaceratops was formally described and name by Michael J. Ryan, Anthony P. Russell and Scott Hartman in 2010 and the type species is Medusaceratops lokii.

facts.statement: The genus name refers to the Greek monster Medusa, alluding to the large, thick, snake-like spikes extending from the sides of its frill.
facts.quote: The generic name refers to Medusa, a monster from Greek mythology whose "hair" consists of snakes and its gaze could turn men to stone, alluding to a unique trait of this genus - the large, thick snake-like spikes that extend to the sides of the frill

facts.statement: The species name lokii honors the Norse god Loki, referencing the years of taxonomic confusion surrounding the fossils before they were named.
facts.quote: The specific name lokii honors Loki, a troublemaking god in the Norse mythology, in reference to the years confusion that surrounded the taxonomic designations of the Mansfield Bonebed material before it was given its own name.

facts.statement: Medusaceratops lived during the Late Cretaceous (middle Campanian stage) in the Judith River Formation of Montana, USA.
facts.quote: Medusaceratops is an extinct genus of centrosaurine ceratopsian dinosaur known from the Late Cretaceous Judith River Formation (middle Campanian stage) of Montana, northern United States.

facts.statement: The dinosaur lived in North America during the Late Cretaceous, approximately between 84 and 71 million years ago.
facts.quote: que vivió a finales del Cretácico, hace aproximadamente entre 84 a 71 millones de años, durante el Campaniense, en lo que hoy es Norteamérica.

facts.statement: New material found in 2011 and 2012 revealed skeletal traits characteristic of Centrosaurinae, confirming the dinosaur's classification.
facts.quote: Chiba et al. in 2017 described new material of Medusaceratops from the Mansfield Bonebed, found in 2011 and 2012 by David Trexler, indicating the presence of traits that were characteristic of Centrosaurinae in the skeleton of M. lokii.

facts.statement: It was once considered the oldest known chasmosaurine until the description of Judiceratops from a slightly older geological formation.
facts.quote: Thus, Medusaceratops was considered to represent the oldest known chasmosaurine, until the naming of Judiceratops by Longrich (2013), also from the Judith River Formation, but from an area equivalent to the lower Oldman Formation or upper Foremost Formation.

facts.statement: The initial interpretation of the frill spikes was challenged in 2018 after additional material was described.
facts.quote: This was challenged in 2018, by the description of additional Mansfield Bonebed material assignable to Medusaceratops.

facts.statement: Further study revealed that the initially identified frill spikes were actually the second through fourth pairs, with the first pair being small and previously misinterpreted.
facts.quote: It became apparent that the 1-3 frill spikes mentioned above are in fact spikes 2–4. The first epiparietal is small and variably procurving and thus was misinterpreted before.

facts.statement: Re-examination showed at least five pairs of frill spikes, a trait consistent with centrosaurines but not chasmosaurines.
facts.quote: At least one more epiparietal pair was also identified (after the fourth), resulting in a total of at least 5 pairs, consistent with centrosaurines like Albertaceratops and Wendiceratops, but not with chasmosaurines.

facts.statement: Medusaceratops is classified within the subfamily Centrosaurinae, where it is most similar to Albertaceratops and Wendiceratops.
facts.quote: Thus, the new study reassigned Medusaceratops to Centrosaurinae, among which it is most similar to Albertaceratops and Wendiceratops.

facts.statement: Medusaceratops belongs to the subfamily Centrosaurinae.
Medusaceratops is distinguished from other contemporaneous ceratopsids by its unique frill ornamentation.
facts.quote: Among valid ceratopsids from the Judith River Formation, Medusaceratops can be directly distinguished from centrosaurine Avaceratops, and chasmosaurines Judiceratops and Spiclypeus based on its unique frill ornamentation.

facts.statement: The genus was formally described and named by Michael J. Ryan, Anthony P. Russell, and Scott Hartman in 2010, with the type species Medusaceratops lokii.
facts.quote: Medusaceratops fue formalmente descrito y nombrado por Michael J. Ryan, Anthony P. Russell y Scott Hartman en 2010 y la especie tipo es Medusaceratops lokii.

facts.statement: The specific name M. lokii honors Loki, a Norse god, referencing the years of taxonomic confusion surrounding the Mansfield Bone Bed material before it received its own name.
facts.quote: El nombre específico M. lokii honra a Loki, un dios problemático en la mitología nórdica, en referencia a la confusión de años que rodeaba las designaciones taxonómicas del material Cama de Hueso Mansfield antes de que se le diera su propio nombre.

facts.statement: The fossil record for Medusaceratops spans from 83.6 to 72.2 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Campanian to Campanian (83.6 to 72.2 million years ago)

facts.statement: Medusaceratops can be distinguished from other valid Judith River ceratopsids like Avaceratops, Judiceratops, and Spiclypeus by its unique frill ornamentation.
facts.quote: Entre los ceratópsidos válidos de la Formación Río Judith, Medusaceratops puede distinguirse directamente de los centrosáurinos Avaceratops, y los casmosaurínos Judiceratops y Spiclypeus en función de su ornamentación de volantes única.

facts.statement: Medusaceratops belongs to the tribe Albertaceratopsini.
